title: Given a `List<Company>` which contains `List<Department>` which contains `List<Employee>`, extract all employee names across all companies.
shortTitle: Given a List<Company> → List<Department> → List<Employee>, extract all employee names across all companies

s1_definition.profdef: This is a multi-level flatten using chained `flatMap` calls, one per level of nesting, followed by a `map` to project the final field. Two levels of nesting — companies containing departments containing employees — require two flatMap steps, then a map to the employee name.
s1_definition.analogy: The group head of the National Bank of India holds several company folders. Each company folder contains department folders, and each department folder contains employee files. She wants one flat list of every employee's name across the whole group. She opens every company, then every department inside it, then pulls the name off every employee file into a single list. Each level of opening is one flatMap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Chain one `flatMap` per level of nesting, then `map` to the field you want.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a multi-level flatten using chained `flatMap` calls, one per level of nesting, followed by a `map` to project the final field. Two levels of nesting — companies containing departments containing employees — require two flatMap steps, then a map to the employee name.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The group head of the National Bank of India holds several company folders. Each company folder contains department folders, and each department folder contains employee files. She wants one flat list of every employee's name across the whole group. She opens every company, then every department inside it, then pulls the name off every employee file into a single list. Each level of opening is one flatMap.

**One line to remember:** Chain one `flatMap` per level of nesting, then `map` to the field you want.

sections.s2_technical:
Each level of nesting needs its own flatMap. Starting from a stream of companies, the first flatMap turns each company into a stream of its departments, giving a flat stream of departments across all companies. The second flatMap turns each department into a stream of its employees, giving a flat stream of employees across all departments across all companies. Finally a map projects each employee to its name.

Concretely the pipeline is companies.stream, then flatMap of company to its departments stream, then flatMap of department to its employees stream, then map of employee to its name, then collect. The rule is simple and memorable: the depth of nesting equals the number of flatMap calls, and the final projection is a plain map because a name is a single value, not a collection.

Thinking about element types at each stage keeps it clear. After the first flatMap the stream is of departments; after the second it is of employees; after the map it is of strings. Tracking the type as it changes stage by stage is the surest way to know how many flatMaps you still need.

A senior nuance: for very deep or dynamic nesting, chained flatMaps stay readable only up to a point, and beyond that a recursive helper or a different data model is clearer. Also, as with single-level flattening, guard any inner collection that might be null so a single bad record does not crash the whole extraction.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is a group with several subsidiary companies, each company has departments, and each department has employees. The group HR head wants one flat list of every employee's name across the entire group for a consolidated headcount report. The data is nested three levels deep. This is exactly how chained flatMap works — one flatMap to flatten companies into departments, another to flatten departments into employees, and a final map to pull out each name.

The code defines `Employee` with a name, `Department` holding employees, and `Company` holding departments. A `GroupReportService` exposes `allEmployeeNames(List<Company>)` using two flatMaps and a map. The runnable `Main` builds two companies with departments and logs all names.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: company NBI Retail with IT (Rajesh, Neha) and Sales (Priya), and company NBI Wealth with Advisory (Amit, Karan).

Step 1: The stream opens over two companies.

Step 2: The first flatMap turns NBI Retail into a stream of its departments IT and Sales, and NBI Wealth into a stream of its one department Advisory. Concatenated, the stream is now IT, Sales, Advisory — a flat stream of departments across both companies.

Step 3: The second flatMap turns each department into a stream of its employees. IT gives Rajesh and Neha, Sales gives Priya, Advisory gives Amit and Karan. Concatenated, the stream is now a flat stream of all five employees.

Step 4: The map projects each employee to its name, so the stream becomes the five name strings.

Step 5: Tracking the type confirms the pipeline: company, then department, then employee, then string.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the five names into one list for the consolidated report.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: List<Company>
    NBI Retail → [IT → [Rajesh, Neha], Sales → [Priya]]
    NBI Wealth → [Advisory → [Amit, Karan]]
    │
    ▼
  stream()  →  Stream<Company>
    │
    ▼
  flatMap(company → departments.stream())   →  Stream<Department> [IT, Sales, Advisory]
    │
    ▼
  flatMap(department → employees.stream())  →  Stream<Employee> [Rajesh,Neha,Priya,Amit,Karan]
    │
    ▼
  map(Employee::getName)  →  Stream<String> ["Rajesh","Neha","Priya","Amit","Karan"]
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [Rajesh, Neha, Priya, Amit, Karan]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To flatten data that is nested several levels deep I chain one flatMap per level and finish with a plain map for the final field. Starting from companies, the first flatMap turns each company into a stream of its departments, giving one flat stream of departments across all companies; the second flatMap turns each department into a stream of its employees, giving one flat stream of all employees; and then a simple map projects each employee to its name.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was a consolidated group headcount. We are a group with several subsidiary companies, each company has departments, and each department has employees, so the data was nested three levels deep, and the group HR head wanted one flat list of every employee's name. Two flatMaps did the flattening and a map pulled out the names.

A senior point I always share is the simple rule I use to get this right every time: the depth of nesting equals the number of flatMap calls, and the final projection is a plain map because a name is a single value, not a collection. I keep it straight by tracking the element type at each stage — company, then department, then employee, then string — which tells me exactly how many flatMaps remain. For very deep or dynamic nesting chained flatMaps stop being readable, and at that point I would switch to a recursive helper or reconsider the data model, and as always I guard any inner list that could be null so one bad record never crashes the whole extraction.
